3 is really tough. My shortlist would be Clarice Starling from Silence of the Lambs, Doc Sportello from Inherent Vice, Vincent Hanna from Heat, JJ Gittes from Chinatown, and Phillip Marlowe from the Long Goodbye. Plenty more that I love, but those 5 stand out for me

Phillip Marlowe as portrayed by Elliot Gould in Altman's The Long Goodbye. Perfect mixture of all things I like in a compelling detective. 

Wisecracking, but focused, down to business. 

Hard boiled, but not too cynical. 

Not a natural born fighter, but scrappy and resourceful when he needs to be. 

Clever and curious, but not some overpowered genius know-it-all that catches everything.

Three examples just popped into my head and they all, weirdly, come from the world of television-

1. *Rustin Cohle, McConaughey, True Detective*. Im really surprised no one has mentioned this yet. Probably the best crime miniseries ever made and the character lives up to that standard. The actors, setting, tone, ambiance etc etc was perfect, the creators just nabbed lightening in a bottle with that project.

2. *Mulder and Scully, David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson, The X Files*.. This series was all over the map when it came to quality but when it got it right it *really* got it right. I think if the show was was nothing more than those two characters in a rental car arguing with one another I would still be in love with it. Their dialogue is so elevated and unnatural but the characters are able to make this unnaturalness become absolutely charming.

3. *Frank Black, Lance Henrikson, Millennium*. Many people missed this series, it only had three seasons but it packed a punch. His character managed to be even darker than McConaugheys but tempered because it was on network television. The series touched on the supernatural, divinity, religious/political/spiritual corruption it really went into all those areas that The XFiles wanted to go but never really could. And, personally, the entire concept behind the Millennium Group was just brilliant, I loved it.
It’s ok with me.
La confidential is a straight up 10/10 film

The Dude in The Big Lebowski. Unwittingly placed in the center of a crime. He's the wrong man for the job. Or any job. But he's out there working the case the best he can.


I also have a guilty pleasure for the buddy cop movies such as Beverly Hills Cop or Lethal Weapon.

Harry Mosby in Arthur Penn's **Night Moves** (1975) is one of my favorite private eyes.  Gene Hackman plays him as a decent man undermined by a culture mired in post-1960s malaise (moral clarity has given away to utter ambiguity).  His own marital troubles have further unmoored him and he eagerly accepts a job to track down a teenage runaway girl who is either in New Mexico or the Florida keys (at least he'll be able to escape Los Angeles for a while).  Things do not go well.

The persona is perfect; confident, charming, intelligent, and resourceful, but enough of a shit that you understand why he’s become adept at swimming in these murky waters. 

He’s also a complete cynic, but I love the subtlety of the backstory. His character has history, but the script doesn’t require any grand emotional monologue or deep character details to convey it. A few brief comments, a few dark reactions from Nicholson, and the weight of his experiences, the cost of his hubris regarding his own intelligence and ability to save the day, and his resulting cynicism and worldview are all perfectly laid out and understood. We don’t need to know any more than that. What happened before in Chinatown is almost like a character maguffin. What happened? He lost somebody. That’s it. It went bad and the man we see in the film is what’s left. It could feel underwritten if the direction and performance weren’t so perfect, but they are, as are the character and the film.

Rust Cohle is one of the greatest characters EVER created, any category. Every time I watch he gets better and better.

Rust Cohle from True Detective Season 1. Very complex and tortured, but retains his acute and keen sense of justice/morality even when he has to go undercover and the lines blur. Spends most of the show philosophizing on existentialism or nihilism, but he can wisecrack with the best of them, too. And, of course, he’s a detective who operates like nobody else in the department has ever seen. Very much a tragic hero who feels like he can’t save himself (or doesn’t believe himself worthy of redemption). I think TD Season 1 is one of the greatest pieces of media ever—tv, movies, music, etc.—and Matthew McConaughey’s performance is a large part of that. Plus it’s just so fucking quotable lol

Cannot believe nobody has mentioned Marge Gunderson from *Fargo* in here.

The Dude in *The Big Lebowski* is an outmatched imbecile who stumbles through the plot just by apparent luck and I guess his sense of cool. Riding the wave is just how he does it, man.

But... Marge? I love how she's so damn confident and capable, which is why it's so hilarious that all of the criminals are inept. The Dude is like her inverse, in that Marge takes most of the film to find the truth because the criminals' ineptitude is so far below *her* detective skills (but maybe a little above Lou's), that they wouldn't possibly seem related. Until she does some of the incredible, prying interviews with locals. She's got such a knack for understanding people, but is sadly just a bit too hopeful to believe that they can be so awful to eachother.
